# Offsite Backup Box

## Overview

One copy of my data lives at my brother's house, in a small noiseless case that sits on a shelf in his spare room. Inside is a single 4 TB drive and a tiny single-board computer, wired to his router with a short cable. The whole box is about the size of a hardback book and draws so little power that he never notices it. It exists for the one disaster I cannot cover locally, the fire or the flood that takes both the live machine and the local copy at the same time. Because it is in a different building, it is already safe from anything that happens inside mine, and because it is a building I trust, it is not exposed to strangers. I do not need it to be fast. I need it to be somewhere else, powered on, and able to receive a copy without my supervision. The box has done that job for three years with almost no attention from me and none at all from him. What I gave up in return is control. I cannot walk over and look at a light when something seems wrong, and I cannot pull a cable to test a theory. So every routine I have around the box is designed to catch a problem over the network, and the alert on my phone is the only symptom I will ever get. That trade is the whole design. A copy in another building is worth more than a clever copy I can reach at a moment's notice, and it costs me one favour and a small amount of monthly checking.

## Setup

I set the box up at his place over one weekend and have not had to touch it physically since. It runs a minimal install with the SSH daemon listening on a non-standard port, and it has its own key, separate from every other key I own, so I can revoke access to it alone without disturbing anything else. My jobs push to it with rsync over SSH twice a week, on a fixed schedule that suits his working hours. The rsync set is trimmed to the directories that actually matter, so the transfer stays small enough to finish inside the window. I put a bandwidth cap on each job so the link never saturates while he is streaming something in the evening.

The plug it hangs from is a small smart plug that reboots the box every fifth night, which clears the occasional wedged process and keeps the uptime honest. I chose the fifth night rather than a fixed weekly moment so the reboot does not always land on the same weekday, which means a long-running job has less chance of always being interrupted at the same point. Both ends run a nightly check that writes a small heartbeat file, and the heartbeat is what tells me the box is still alive. If two heartbeats in a row are missing I get an alert on my phone, and nine times out of ten a power-cycle from the plug app fixes it. The key and the port live in the password manager, so a rebuild is a known set of steps instead of an archaeology project. Before I handed the box over I wrote a one-page note for my brother, with a photograph of the case, a description of the little light, and my phone number, so that if something looks wrong he knows who to tell and is not left wondering whether it matters. That page is stuck inside the cupboard door beside the shelf, and it has never been needed, which is exactly what I wanted from it.

## Maintenance

Once a month I pull one file back from the box over the network and open it, just to prove the copy is readable rather than merely present. I pick a file at random from the most recent set and I check that it opens without fuss. I also read the heartbeat log from the last four weeks and confirm there is no gap, because a silent box is the failure I fear most, and a box that has stopped sending heartbeats is a box I only think is working. Every few months I ask my brother to glance at the case and confirm the little light is on, which is a crude but effective check and costs him nothing. The bandwidth cap gets reviewed whenever his household adds another person streaming video. I keep notes on the drive's age beside the serial, so I can replace it before it becomes the thing that fails on the worst night. I also test the restore side rather than only the send side once a season, by fetching a whole small directory and comparing its file count with the count on the live machine, because a copy that arrives in a form I cannot unpack is not a copy at all. That test takes ten minutes and it is the one I would keep if I had to give up every other routine.

## Notes

The best part of the arrangement is that a reboot solves almost everything. When a job fails now I power-cycle the plug from my desk and wait five minutes before looking any deeper, and most of the time that is the end of it. I was nervous about asking a favour this large, but my brother has been relaxed about it, and the box makes no sound and no light where he sleeps. I keep the data set small on purpose. A box holding everything is harder to justify than one holding the few directories I could not bear to lose, and a small set also finishes inside the window without stretching his link. If the drive ever fails I already know which drive to buy, and I have told my brother that a dead box is not a crisis, just a postcard to post to me, because I would rather he told me than quietly unplugged it. The one thing I would warn anyone about is the drive. A single drive in a single case has no redundancy at all, so the box is a copy, not a system, and I treat it as the last line rather than the first. If it dies I will know from the heartbeats, and the data on it will still exist in the other two places until I fit a new drive and let it catch up.
